Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The Sri Lankan army launched an operation against Tamil rebels in the country's north early Monday, the military said, claiming to have rescued thousands of civilians trapped in a government safe zone. The Sri Lankan army has relaunched its attacks on Tamil rebels in the country's north. A rebel Web site, TamilNet, said government forces were engaged in a fresh ground offensive. A TamilNet correspondent in Vanni reported heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire. Thirty civilians died in shelling Sunday, rebels said. The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. "Thousands of civilians who had been forcibly held by the LTTE terrorists in the government declared No Fire Zone (NFZ) were rescued early hours this morning, 20 April, as the troops engaged in a massive scale rescue mission, were able to open a safe passage for the civilians," the Ministry of Defense Web site said. More than 10,000 civilians are trying to seek refuge with soldiers, the military said. The upsurge in hostilities follows a two-day cessation last week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year. The U.S. State Department on Thursday called for a cease-fire between the Sri Lankan government and Tamil Tigers to allow civilians to escape the fighting. "We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out," acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. "Both sides must immediately return to a humanitarian pause and both must respect the right of free movement of those civilian men, women and children trapped by the fighting."  Watch the heavy toll of fighting on civilians » . A brief cessation of hostilities  announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 allowed the United Nations and its partners to bring in aid, but a renewed government offensive has left civilians trapped in a war zone. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and his humanitarian chief John Holmes called the brief halt in fighting inadequate and have pushed for a longer humanitarian pause in fighting. The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is the fact that more than 100,000 people are crowded in a "very small pocket of land" that is about five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people," Holmes told reporters Wednesday. Overcrowding is also a problem in camps housing displaced people, according to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). As of Monday, some 65,000 displaced people were crammed into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, with 35,000 more expected to arrive within 48 hours, the organization said in a statement. ' UNICEF said it feared for children trapped in the escalating fighting and is worried that the worst is yet to come. The group appealed for donations to help cover "the most immediate needs of the affected population in health and nutrition, water and sanitation, protection and education." The crowded population, primarily comprised of Tamil civilians, is subject to the continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers released a joint statement as well on Wednesday, saying that the Tamil Tigers are using Tamil civilians as human shields. The Tigers have been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983. The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that it has helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and injured patients, and their caregivers, from Putumattalan in rebel-held territory since February. "These evacuations have saved many lives," said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. "It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan." The Red Cross says there's an acute shortage of medical supplies in the region, which it is trying to rectify.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- The Sri Lankan army launched a renewed operation against Tamil rebels in the country’s north early Monday, the military said, claiming that it had rescued thousands of civilians trapped in a government-designated safe zone.

TamilNet, a rebel website, reported that government forces were engaged in a fresh ground offensive. A TamilNet correspondent in Vanni described heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire. Rebels said 30 civilians were killed in shelling Sunday.

The Sri Lankan government has been fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years.

“Thousands of civilians who had been forcibly held by the LTTE terrorists in the government-declared No Fire Zone (NFZ) were rescued early hours this morning, 20 April, as the troops engaged in a massive-scale rescue mission were able to open a safe passage for the civilians,” the Ministry of Defense website said.

More than 10,000 civilians were attempting to seek refuge with soldiers, according to the military.

The escalation in hostilities followed a two-day cessation the previous week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year.

On Thursday, the U.S. State Department called for a cease-fire between the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tigers to allow civilians to escape the fighting.

“We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out,” acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. “Both sides must immediately return to a humanitarian pause, and both must respect the right of free movement of those civilian men, women and children trapped by the fighting.”

Watch the heavy toll of fighting on civilians »

A brief cessation of hostilities announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 allowed the United Nations and its partners to deliver aid, but a renewed government offensive left civilians trapped in a war zone.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and his humanitarian chief, John Holmes, called the brief halt in fighting inadequate and pressed for a longer humanitarian pause.

According to Holmes, the most urgent concern was that more than 100,000 people were crowded into a “very small pocket of land” measuring about five square miles—roughly twice the size of New York’s Central Park.

“It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people,” Holmes told reporters Wednesday.

Overcrowding was also a problem in camps housing displaced people, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). As of Monday, approximately 65,000 displaced people were crammed into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, with an additional 35,000 expected to arrive within 48 hours, the organization said in a statement.

UNICEF said it feared for children trapped amid the escalating fighting and was concerned that the worst was yet to come. The organization appealed for donations to help meet “the most immediate needs of the affected population in health and nutrition, water and sanitation, protection and education.”

The densely concentrated population, composed primarily of Tamil civilians, remained exposed to continuing Sri Lankan government assaults.

The British and French foreign ministers also issued a joint statement Wednesday, saying that the Tamil Tigers were using Tamil civilians as human shields.

The Tigers have been designated a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States, as well as by the European Union.

As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that, since February, it had helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and injured patients and their caregivers from Putumattalan, in rebel-held territory.

“These evacuations have saved many lives,” said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. “It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan.”

The Red Cross said the region faced an acute shortage of medical supplies, a situation it was working to address.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Sri Lanka’s military said it began a new operation against Tamil insurgents in the north of the country early Monday and claimed that thousands of civilians confined within a government-designated safe area had been freed.

TamilNet, a website aligned with the rebels, also reported that government troops had started another ground assault. Its correspondent in Vanni described intense artillery bombardment, rocket attacks and gunfire. The rebels said shelling on Sunday killed 30 civilians.

For nearly 25 years, the Sri Lankan government had been engaged in a civil war with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

According to a statement on the Defense Ministry’s website, troops conducting a large-scale rescue effort opened a secure route early on April 20 for thousands of civilians whom the ministry said had been forcibly detained by the LTTE inside the government-declared No Fire Zone. The military added that more than 10,000 people were attempting to reach soldiers for safety.

The renewed violence came after a two-day pause the previous week marking the Sinhala and Hindu New Year.

On Thursday, the U.S. State Department urged both the Sri Lankan authorities and the Tamil Tigers to halt the fighting so civilians could leave the combat zone.

Acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement that the government, military and Tamil Tigers should immediately suspend hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area had been safely evacuated. He said both parties needed to restore a humanitarian pause at once and respect the freedom of movement of the men, women and children caught in the fighting.

A short suspension announced by Sri Lanka’s government on April 12 enabled the United Nations and partner organizations to deliver assistance. However, the government’s subsequent offensive again left civilians stranded in an active war zone.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and humanitarian chief John Holmes said the temporary stoppage was insufficient and pressed for a longer humanitarian break.

Holmes said the most urgent issue was that over 100,000 people were packed into a tiny area of roughly five square miles—about twice the size of New York City’s Central Park. Speaking to reporters Wednesday, he emphasized that the territory was extremely small for what the United Nations believed to be such a large population.

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said overcrowding was also affecting camps for displaced residents. By Monday, approximately 65,000 people had been squeezed into facilities in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, and another 35,000 were expected within the following 48 hours.

UNICEF expressed particular concern for children caught in the intensifying conflict and warned that conditions could deteriorate further. It requested donations to address the population’s most urgent requirements, including health care and nutrition, clean water and sanitation, protection and education.

The densely concentrated civilians—most of them Tamils—remained exposed to continuing attacks by Sri Lankan government forces.

In a joint statement issued Wednesday, the British and French foreign ministers also accused the Tamil Tigers of using Tamil civilians as human shields.

Thirty-two countries, including the United States, as well as the European Union, had designated the Tigers as a terrorist organization. Up to 70,000 people had died since the war formally started in 1983.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that, since February, it had assisted in evacuating more than 10,000 ill and wounded patients and their caregivers from Putumattalan, an area under rebel control.

Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka, said those evacuations had preserved many lives and needed to continue because sick and injured people were arriving daily at Putumattalan’s improvised medical centers.

The Red Cross also reported a severe shortage of medical supplies in the area and said it was working to remedy the problem.
outputs.L3:
The Sri Lankan army resumed its offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels in the north of the country following a two-day pause for the holidays. The renewed fighting marked another escalation in the nearly 25-year civil conflict between government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

Military officials said government forces had opened a safe passage from a government-declared No Fire Zone and rescued thousands of civilians who, according to the authorities, had been held there by the LTTE. More than 10,000 people were reportedly seeking refuge with government soldiers as they fled the shrinking rebel-held territory.

Reports from the conflict zone, however, described intense violence. The pro-rebel website TamilNet reported heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire, while the rebels claimed that 30 civilians had been killed in shelling on Sunday. Independent verification of casualty figures and battlefield claims remained difficult because access to the area was severely restricted.

Amid growing concern over the humanitarian situation, the United States called for an immediate cease-fire. U.S. officials said a halt in the fighting was necessary to allow more than 140,000 civilians believed to be trapped in the conflict zone to escape safely and gain access to urgently needed humanitarian assistance.
outputs.L4:
Sri Lankan government forces launched a renewed offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels in the north of the country, saying the operation was intended to open a safe route for civilians trapped in the conflict zone. The military said troops had breached rebel defenses and created a passage out of the government-declared no-fire zone, where tens of thousands of people had been confined as fighting intensified.

According to military officials, thousands of civilians escaped through the newly opened corridor, while more than 10,000 people sought refuge in government-controlled territory. Officials described the operation as a rescue effort aimed at separating civilians from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, whom the government accused of preventing people from leaving. The rebels disputed the government’s account and accused the military of endangering civilians through continued attacks.

Reports from the area described heavy shelling and mounting casualties, although limited access for journalists and aid agencies made the claims difficult to verify independently. Humanitarian organizations warned that civilians lacked adequate food, clean water, shelter, and medical care. Hospitals and temporary treatment centers were reportedly struggling to cope with the wounded.

Despite the reported escapes, more than 140,000 civilians were still believed to be in danger as government troops pressed deeper into the shrinking rebel-held territory. Aid groups expressed particular concern that renewed combat in and around the no-fire zone could cause further large-scale loss of life.

The escalation intensified international pressure on both sides to halt the fighting. Foreign governments and humanitarian organizations called for an immediate cease-fire to allow civilians to leave safely and relief supplies to reach those who remained trapped. They also urged the LTTE to permit unrestricted civilian departures and asked the Sri Lankan military to avoid using heavy weapons in populated areas.

The government maintained that it was close to defeating the LTTE after decades of civil war and rejected calls that it said would give the rebels time to regroup. Nevertheless, the deteriorating humanitarian situation left civilians caught between advancing government forces and the remaining Tiger fighters, raising fears that the final stage of the conflict could become its deadliest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the Sri Lankan army’s April 20 offensive against the Tamil Tigers and the evacuation of civilians from the No Fire Zone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lankan troops breach rebel defenses as thousands flee war zone**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, April 20, 2009** — Sri Lankan troops launched a major offensive Monday against the Tamil Tigers’ shrinking coastal enclave, opening an escape route that the government said allowed tens of thousands of civilians to leave the designated No Fire Zone.

Military officials said soldiers breached an earthen barrier built by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, near Puthukkudiyiruppu in northeastern Sri Lanka. Government television showed crowds crossing shallow water and moving toward army-held territory, many carrying children and a few possessions.

The government said more than 35,000 people had escaped by Monday afternoon, though the figure could not be independently verified because journalists and most aid organizations were barred from the combat area.

Sri Lankan authorities accused the Tigers of holding civilians as human shields and firing on those trying to leave. The LTTE had previously denied deliberately preventing civilians from escaping and accused the military of shelling populated areas.

Aid agencies warned that people trapped inside the narrow coastal strip faced severe shortages of food, medicine and clean water. The United Nations and humanitarian groups repeatedly called on both sides to protect civilians and urged the rebels to allow them to leave freely.

The military said the offensive was aimed at separating civilians from the remaining Tiger fighters as government forces closed in on the group’s last territory. Officials described the operation as a rescue mission, but human-rights organizations expressed concern that heavy fighting in such a densely populated area could cause significant civilian casualties.

The No Fire Zone had been declared by the government as a refuge for civilians, although reports of shelling and gunfire inside the area raised questions about its safety. Independent casualty estimates remained difficult to establish.

The LTTE had fought since 1983 for an independent Tamil homeland in Sri Lanka’s north and east, saying the ethnic Tamil minority faced discrimination under successive governments dominated by the Sinhalese majority. By April 2009, the rebels had lost nearly all the territory they once controlled and were surrounded along a small section of the northeastern coast.

Monday’s mass evacuation appeared to mark a decisive stage in the 26-year conflict, but officials and relief workers warned that thousands of civilians remained in danger as fighting continued.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed breaking-news article on renewed fighting in northern Sri Lanka after the Sinhala and Hindu New Year pause, incorporating statements from the military, TamilNet, the U.S. State Department, the United Nations, UNICEF, and the Red Cross.
counterfactuals.output:
**Renewed fighting reported in northern Sri Lanka after New Year pause ends**

*COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — April 15, 2009* — Heavy fighting resumed in northern Sri Lanka after a two-day government-declared pause for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year expired, as international agencies warned that civilians trapped between government troops and the Tamil Tiger rebels faced an increasingly desperate humanitarian crisis.

Sri Lanka’s military said operations against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, restarted after midnight in the coastal pocket of Mullaitivu District still controlled by the rebels. Military officials said troops were trying to open routes for civilians to leave while completing their offensive against the remaining Tiger forces.

The government described the holiday pause as an opportunity for civilians to cross into military-held territory. It accused the LTTE of preventing families from leaving and using the lull to reinforce defensive positions. The military said rebels fired toward government lines during or immediately after the pause.

TamilNet, a pro-Tamil news website that has frequently carried reports sympathetic to the LTTE, gave a sharply different account. It reported renewed artillery and mortar fire in the densely populated enclave and alleged that civilians had been killed or wounded. TamilNet said the pause had not provided sufficient time or security for aid to reach displaced families.

Neither the military’s battlefield claims nor TamilNet’s casualty reports could be independently verified. Journalists and most international observers were barred from the combat area, and communications with people inside the enclave were severely restricted.

### International pressure for a longer halt

The United States urged both sides to protect civilians and called for an end to the fighting.

The U.S. State Department said the LTTE should release civilians, lay down its weapons and stop using populated areas for military purposes. It also pressed the Sri Lankan government to end shelling near civilians and allow humanitarian organizations access to those trapped in the conflict zone.

Washington said the brief New Year pause had not been enough to resolve the humanitarian emergency and urged the parties to establish conditions under which civilians could leave safely.

United Nations officials similarly expressed concern that the two-day suspension was too short. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had appealed for the pause to be extended and for a U.N. humanitarian team to be allowed into the conflict area.

The United Nations estimated that tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in a shrinking strip of land along the northeastern coast. Officials warned that shortages of food, drinking water, medicine and shelter were becoming critical.

The U.N. accused the LTTE of restricting civilian movement and recruiting people, including children, for the fighting. At the same time, it repeatedly called on the government to avoid using heavy weapons in areas containing large numbers of displaced people.

### Children at particular risk

UNICEF said children were among those most endangered by the renewed combat. The agency warned that families in the enclave were living in overcrowded makeshift shelters with inadequate sanitation, nutrition and medical care.

UNICEF also reiterated its opposition to the recruitment and use of children by armed groups. It called for children and their families to be allowed to leave the combat zone without obstruction and for all parties to respect international humanitarian law.

Aid officials said malnutrition, disease and untreated wounds posed mounting dangers even for civilians not directly struck by gunfire or shelling. Medical facilities inside the enclave were reported to be overwhelmed and short of anesthetics, antibiotics, blood and basic surgical supplies.

### Red Cross evacuations under strain

The International Committee of the Red Cross remained one of the few international organizations able to maintain limited contact with the conflict area. Working with local Red Cross personnel, it had organized sea evacuations of wounded and sick civilians from the northeastern coast.

The ICRC said humanitarian workers needed safe and regular access to the population. It called on both the government and the LTTE to protect civilians, medical workers and patients, and to permit the evacuation of people requiring urgent treatment.

Red Cross officials warned that humanitarian operations could not keep pace with the scale of need. Sea transfers were vulnerable to weather, security conditions and interruptions in access, while medical teams inside the enclave faced severe shortages.

### Conflicting accounts of civilian movement

Sri Lankan authorities said thousands of civilians had escaped Tiger-held territory and were being taken to government-run displacement camps. The government maintained that the final offensive was intended to free civilians and eliminate the LTTE’s remaining military leadership.

Human-rights and aid organizations, however, raised concerns both about civilians trapped under Tiger control and about conditions and freedom of movement in the camps established by the government.

The LTTE, which had fought since the 1980s for an independent Tamil state in the north and east, rejected demands for unconditional surrender. Its territory had by then been reduced to a narrow coastal enclave after months of rapid government advances.

With independent access to the battlefield blocked, the full scale of the renewed fighting and civilian casualties remained unclear. But statements from the United Nations, UNICEF, the Red Cross and the United States reflected a common warning: without a longer ceasefire and reliable humanitarian access, civilians would continue to bear the brunt of the war’s final phase.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the humanitarian crisis during the final stages of Sri Lanka’s civil war, including civilian casualties, overcrowded displacement camps, calls for a cease-fire, and shortages of medical supplies.
counterfactuals.output:
In the final months of Sri Lanka’s civil war, especially from January to May 2009, hundreds of thousands of civilians were trapped in a shrinking area of the northern Vanni region between government forces and the Tamil Tigers (LTTE). Heavy shelling and fighting—including in designated “No Fire Zones” and near hospitals—caused extensive civilian deaths and injuries. The LTTE was also accused of preventing civilians from escaping, forcibly recruiting people, and firing from civilian areas. Casualty figures remain disputed: a later UN review estimated that as many as 40,000 civilians may have been killed, while other estimates vary substantially.

Hospitals and makeshift clinics were overwhelmed and repeatedly displaced. Doctors reported severe shortages of anesthetics, antibiotics, blood, surgical equipment, food, and clean water, forcing treatment under extremely difficult conditions. Humanitarian access was sharply restricted.

After escaping the combat zone, roughly 280,000 displaced people were held in heavily guarded, overcrowded camps, most notably the Manik Farm complex. Residents faced inadequate sanitation, shelter, medical care, and family tracing, while restrictions on movement raised concerns about prolonged internment.

The UN, humanitarian organizations, foreign governments, and human-rights groups repeatedly called for a cease-fire or humanitarian pause, protection of civilians, unrestricted aid access, and permission for civilians to leave. The Sri Lankan government rejected a full cease-fire, arguing it would allow the LTTE to regroup, and declared victory in May 2009. The conduct of both sides—particularly alleged indiscriminate government attacks and LTTE use of civilians as human shields—has remained the subject of war-crimes and accountability demands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an international news story reporting that Sri Lankan troops claim to have rescued thousands of civilians held by the LTTE, while rebels allege heavy shelling and civilian deaths.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lankan troops say thousands rescued as rebels allege civilian deaths**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka —** Sri Lankan troops have rescued thousands of civilians from territory controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, the government said, as rebel officials accused the military of heavy shelling that killed civilians in the shrinking war zone.

Military officials said civilians crossed into government-held areas after troops breached rebel defenses in the northeast, where the LTTE has been confined by a major army offensive. The government described the movement as a large-scale escape and accused the separatist group of holding civilians as human shields.

The LTTE disputed that account, saying civilians were fleeing intense artillery fire and alleging that shells had struck densely populated areas. Rebel representatives reported numerous civilian casualties but provided no independently confirmed figures.

The claims from both sides could not be independently verified because access to the conflict zone remains severely restricted. Aid agencies have repeatedly expressed concern about civilians trapped in the area, warning of shortages of food, medicine and safe shelter.

Sri Lanka’s government has denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its forces are conducting operations intended to minimize casualties. It has called on the rebels to surrender and release civilians. The LTTE, which has fought for an independent Tamil state for decades, accuses the government of disregarding civilian lives.

International organizations and foreign governments have urged both sides to protect noncombatants and allow humanitarian assistance into the area. The latest developments come as government forces appear close to defeating the rebels militarily, potentially bringing an end to one of Asia’s longest-running civil wars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a report titled “Sri Lankan army launches operation against Tamil rebels,” explaining the renewed offensive, the plight of more than 100,000 trapped civilians, international demands for a humanitarian pause, and Red Cross evacuation efforts.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sri Lankan army launches operation against Tamil rebels

The Sri Lankan army has renewed its offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels in the northeast after a temporary halt intended to allow civilians to leave the conflict zone.

Government forces said the operation was aimed at rescuing civilians and defeating the remaining fighters of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who had been confined to a narrow coastal strip. The government accused the rebels of preventing people from escaping and using them as human shields—an allegation the LTTE denied.

More than 100,000 civilians were believed to be trapped in the shrinking rebel-held area, where food, clean water and medical supplies were running dangerously low. Aid agencies warned that makeshift hospitals were overwhelmed and that continued fighting could cause heavy civilian casualties. Independent access to the battlefield remained severely restricted, making claims from either side difficult to verify.

The United Nations and foreign governments called for an immediate humanitarian pause. They urged both sides to protect civilians, allow aid into the area and provide safe passage for those wishing to leave. International officials also pressed the LTTE to release civilians and called on Sri Lankan forces to avoid using heavy weapons near densely populated areas.

The International Committee of the Red Cross continued efforts to evacuate wounded and sick civilians by sea. Red Cross vessels transported patients and accompanying relatives from the conflict zone to government-controlled territory, while also delivering limited medical supplies. The organization said the evacuations offered a vital lifeline but could not meet the scale of the humanitarian need.

Sri Lankan authorities rejected calls for a longer ceasefire, arguing that any extended pause would allow the rebels to regroup. Humanitarian organizations warned, however, that without a break in the fighting and reliable access for relief workers, civilians would remain in extreme danger.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
